> ## How to use this worksheet
>
> There are **four sections**:
>
> 1.  **Read in the data and look at it** — all 64 needles first, then the 8 tree means. No tests, just plots
> 2.  **One-sample t-test** — is one group different from a fixed number? (plus the one-tailed variation)
> 3.  **Two-sample t-test** — are the two sides different from each other?
> 4.  **Paired t-test** — is each *tree* different on its two sides?
>
> Work through them in order. Type every line of code yourself into the **script skeleton** — do not copy-paste from this worksheet. Blocks marked **▶ Run this** are code you type and execute. Blocks marked **✏️ Your turn** are for you to write in, by hand, on this sheet.

It already has the `# ── Part …` headers laid out in order, and the blocks you have typed a dozen times — setup, reading the data, averaging away pseudoreplication, the `summarize()` block — are filled in for you. Everything else is blank, and that blank space is the lesson. Work down the worksheet and type your code under the matching header.
>
> **Type the `# ── Part …` header comment at the top of each block, too.** Those comment lines are not decoration — they are how your script stays navigable, how you find your way back to a block that broke, and how I find your work when I read your script.

## Column names in `pine_data.csv` / `pine_data.xlsx`

Both files hold the **same six columns, with exactly these names**. Type them exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and `Needle_Length` or `needle_length` will not work:

| Column | What it is |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `source_file` | the raw team file the row came from |
| `team` | field team — one team = **one tree** |
| `replicate` | needle number within a tree side (1-8) |
| `side` | sun exposure — `"shady"` or `"sunny"` |
| `needle_length_mm` | needle length, millimetres |
| `needle_width_mm` | needle width, millimetres |

After you read the file in, click `pine_df` in the **Variables** pane in Positron and check the names on your screen against this table before you write any other code.
:::

# Section 1 · Read In the Data and Look at It

## 1.1 · Setup

Download the **tools script** from the button at the top. In your project folder, make a new folder called **`themes_functions`** and save the file into it, so the path is `themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R`.

That is a *different* folder from `scripts/` — `scripts/` holds the code **you** write, `themes_functions/` holds tools you `source()` and do not edit.

One `source()` line then gives you two things you will use for the rest of the semester:

- `theme_regular()` — the publication theme from the Graphing lecture
- `summary_stats()` — hand it a column of numbers, get back `n` / `mean` / `sd` / `se` and a 95% CI

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)   # round_half_up(), used inside summary_stats()
library(car)       # leveneTest()

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** `source()` needs the path to be right. If R says *cannot open file*, that is exactly what it is telling you — check that the folder is called `themes_functions`, spelled exactly that way, and that it sits next to your `.Rproj` file.

> 💡 **You do not need `glimpse()` or `head()`.** Click `pine_df` in the **Variables** pane in Positron and look at it there.

## 1.2 · Look at all the data — spread

Before we do anything clever, look at **every needle we measured** — all 64 rows, exactly as they came out of the field.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.2 · Boxplot of all the raw needles ───────────────────────────
raw_box_plot <- pine_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(side, needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08)) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10)

raw_box_plot
```

> 💡 **Why `position_jitter()` here?** 32 needles land on a single x value, so a plain `geom_point()` would stack them into a line and hide the duplicates. Jitter nudges them sideways so you can see how many there are.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.3 · Mean and SE of all the raw needles ───────────────────────
raw_mean_se_plot <- pine_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(side, needle_length_mm)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2) +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10)

raw_mean_se_plot
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out — those error bars are a lie.** They are computed as SD / √n with **n = 32** per side. But we did not measure 32 independent things. We measured **4 trees**, eight needles each. The 32 is fake, so the precision is fake. Hold this picture in your head — we fix it next and then plot it again.

## 1.4 · Average out the pseudoreplication

The 8 needles from one side of one tree are **pseudoreplicates** — they are not 8 independent measurements, they are 8 looks at the same tree side. Average them so each tree side is **one** data point.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.4 · Average out pseudoreplication ────────────────────────────
p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

p_df
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** 64 rows became 8. That is not data loss — it is the correct sample size. We measured 8 needles per side, but only **4 trees**.

✏️ **Your turn:** What is our true sample unit here — needles? branches? trees? tree sides? Why does that matter for the rest of this worksheet?


## 1.5 · Summary statistics, the long way

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.5 · Summary stats the long way ───────────────────────────────
stats_df <- p_df %>%
  group_by(side) %>%
  summarize(
    n    = sum(!is.na(needle_length_mm)),
    mean = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    se   = sd / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stats_df
```

## 1.6 · Summary statistics, the short way

The exact same numbers, from the function you `source()`d in Part 1.1:

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.6 · Summary stats with summary_stats() ───────────────────────
summary_stats(p_df$needle_length_mm)                 # all 8 trees together

p_df %>% group_by(side) %>% reframe(summary_stats(needle_length_mm))
```

> 💡 **Why `reframe()`?** `summarize()` wants **one value** per group. `summary_stats()` hands back a whole **row** — six columns at once — so `reframe()` is the verb that allows it. The `group_by()` in front is the same one you already know.

::: callout-important
## Degrees of freedom — read this before Sections 2, 3 and 4

**df = the number of values free to vary once you have estimated a mean.** You lose one df for every mean you estimate. Our data is **4 trees, one shady side and one sunny side each** — so n is always *trees*, never needles.

| Test | What n counts | df formula | Our df |
|:-------------------|:--------------|:-----------------|:------:|
| One-sample (Section 2) | trees in the one group | n − 1 | **3** |
| Two-sample (Section 3) | trees in both groups | n₁ + n₂ − 2 | **6** |
| Welch's (Section 3) | both groups, penalised | Welch–Satterthwaite | **≈ 5.66** |
| Paired (Section 4) | **differences** | n~pairs~ − 1 | **3** |

Check the `df =` line in every bit of `t.test()` output below against this table. If it does not match, you ran a different test than you thought you did.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Section 2 · One-Sample t-Test

**▶ Run this:**

``` r

shady_df
```

## 2.5 · The one-tailed variation

Your prediction in Part 2.2 probably had a **direction** — shady needles are *shorter* than 15 mm. If you committed to that direction **before** collecting data, you can put all 5% of α into one tail.

✏️ **Your turn:** Write the one-tailed hypotheses.

```

```

**▶ Run this** — `alternative` is the only thing that changes:

``` r
# ── Part 2.5 · One-sample t-test, one-tailed ────────────────────────────
one_tailed_model <- t.test(shady_df$needle_length_mm, mu = 15, alternative = "less")

one_tailed_model
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** Choosing the tail **after** looking at your means is not a one-tailed test. It is a two-tailed test with the p-value secretly halved, and it is one of the most common ways people accidentally cheat. Pick the direction from the biology, before you collect data, or use two-tailed.

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** A one-tailed test is defensible when a result in the opposite direction would lead to the **same action** as no result at all — a drug that harms patients and a drug that does nothing are both "do not approve." For our pine needles, is "sunny is longer" *and* "shady is longer" both interesting biology? So which should we use?

## 3.2 · Check normality within each group

**▶ Run this:**

``` r

    shapiro_p = shapiro.test(needle_length_mm)$p.value,
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** With n = 4, Shapiro-Wilk has almost no power — it will pass nearly anything. A high p-value here is not evidence that the data are normal; it is evidence that we do not have enough data to tell. Run it, report it, but lean on the design and the biology.

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early — compute the t-statistic by hand** and confirm it matches `t.test()`:

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{S_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}$$

``` r
# ── Part 3.6 · Two-sample t by hand ─────────────────────────────────────
sunny_df <- p_df %>% filter(side == "sunny")   # shady_df is from Part 2.1

n1 <- length(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
n2 <- length(sunny_df$needle_length_mm)
s1 <- sd(shady_df$needle_length_mm)
s2 <- sd(sunny_df$needle_length_mm)

sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * s1^2 + (n2 - 1) * s2^2) / (n1 + n2 - 2))

(mean(shady_df$needle_length_mm) - mean(sunny_df$needle_length_mm)) /
  (sp * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2))
```

Look at the denominator of `sp`: `n1 + n2 - 2`. That **is** the degrees of freedom. df is not a rule to memorise — it is whatever you divided by.
:::

# Section 4 · Paired t-Test

A paired t-test compares two measurements taken from the **same** subject — here, the sunny side and the shady side of the *same* tree. It uses the **differences** between pairs as the data.

## 4.1 · Question, prediction, hypotheses

Notice that H₀ and Hₐ are now about **one number**: the mean difference.

✏️ **Your turn:**

```         
Question (the biology, in plain English):

____________________________________________________________________


Prediction (what you expect, and WHY):

____________________________________________________________________

____________________________________________________________________


H0 (in terms of the mean difference between the two sides of a tree):

____________________________________________________________________


Ha:

____________________________________________________________________


alpha = ____________
```

## 4.2 · Reshape and run the test

`t.test()` needs the two sides side by side, one row per tree.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.2 · Paired t-test ────────────────────────────────────────────
p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side, values_from = needle_length_mm)

p_wide_df

paired_model <- t.test(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)

paired_model
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out — order matters for the sign.** `t.test(shady, sunny, paired = TRUE)` computes **shady − sunny**. Swap the two and `t` flips sign. The p-value is identical, but the direction you report is backwards. Always write down which way you subtracted.

✏️ **Your turn:** Copy the numbers out, and note the df.

```

mean difference = ________ mm     (this is ________ minus ________)
```

## 4.4 · A paired test *is* a one-sample test

Treat the **shady side as each tree's own control** and compute one difference per tree.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.4 · Paired = one-sample on the differences ───────────────────
diff_df <- p_wide_df %>%
  mutate(difference = sunny - shady)

diff_df

diff_model <- t.test(diff_df$difference, mu = 0)

diff_model
```

# Take-Home Extension — Mouse Body Mass and the Island Rule

*Due Monday, September 28 — before the Power & Error class.*

This uses the same machinery you just ran, on a new dataset and a new question. This time **you** decide which test to run and defend that choice; nobody walks you through it.

## Background

The **Island Rule** predicts that when mainland species colonize islands, small-bodied species — like rodents — tend to evolve larger body size, released from mainland predation and competition. Below are body mass measurements for deer mice trapped on Sidney Island (island) and near Vancouver, BC (mainland).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Take-home extension ──────────────────────────────────────
mice_df <- read_csv("data/mice_weights.csv")

mice_df %>% group_by(location) %>% reframe(summary_stats(mass_g))
```

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`, `library(janitor)`, `library(car)`, and `source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")`? Spelling? A missing `)` or `%>%` at the *start* of a line?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.
